Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant
Responsibility Act of 1996, Section 102,
Pub. L. 104-208, Div. C, 110 Stat. 3009-546
(codified at 8 U.S.C. § 1103 note), as Amended
1a

Section 102 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of
1996 (“IIRIRA”), Pub. L. 104-208, Div. C, 110 Stat. 3009-546 (codified at 8 U.S.C.
§ 1103 note), as amended.
(a) In General.—The Secretary of Homeland Security shall take such actions as may
be necessary to install additional physical barriers and roads (including the removal
of obstacles to detection of illegal entrants) in the vicinity of the United States border
to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry into the United States.
(b) Construction of Fencing and Road Improvements Along the Border.—
(1) Additional fencing along southwest border.—
(A) Reinforced fencing.—In carrying out subsection (a), the Secretary of
Homeland Security shall construct reinforced fencing along not less
than 700 miles of the southwest border where fencing would be most
practical and effective and provide for the installation of additional
physical barriers, roads, lighting, cameras, and sensors to gain
operational control of the southwest border.
(B) Priority areas.—In carrying out this section [amending this section],
the Secretary of Homeland Security shall—
(i) identify the 370 miles, or other mileage determined by the
Secretary, whose authority to determine other mileage shall
expire on December 31, 2008, along the southwest border where
fencing would be most practical and effective in deterring
smugglers and aliens attempting to gain illegal entry into the
United States; and
(ii) not later than December 31, 2008, complete construction of
reinforced fencing along the miles identified under clause (i).
(C) Consultation.—
(i) In general.—In carrying out this section, the Secretary of
Homeland Security shall consult with the Secretary of the
Interior, the Secretary of Agriculture, States, local governments,
Indian tribes, and property owners in the United States to
minimize the impact on the environment, culture, commerce, and
quality of life for the communities and residents located near the
sites at which such fencing is to be constructed.
2a

(ii) Savings provision.—Nothing in this subparagraph may be
construed to—
(I) create or negate any right of action for a State, local
government, or other person or entity affected by this
subsection; or
(II) affect the eminent domain laws of the United States or
of any State.
(D) Limitation on requirements.—Notwithstanding subparagraph (A),
nothing in this paragraph shall require the Secretary of Homeland
Security to install fencing, physical barriers, roads, lighting, cameras,
and sensors in a particular location along an international border of the
United States, if the Secretary determines that the use or placement of
such resources is not the most appropriate means to achieve and
maintain operational control over the international border at such
location.
(2) Prompt acquisition of necessary easements.—The Attorney General, acting
under the authority conferred in section 103(b) of the Immigration and
Nationality Act [8 U.S.C. 1103(b)] (as inserted by subsection (d)), shall
promptly acquire such easements as may be necessary to carry out this
subsection and shall commence construction of fences immediately following
such acquisition (or conclusion of portions thereof).
(3) Safety features.—The Attorney General, while constructing the additional
fencing under this subsection, shall incorporate such safety features into the
design of the fence system as are necessary to ensure the well-being of border
patrol agents deployed within or in near proximity to the system.
(4) Authorization of appropriations.—There are authorized to be appropriated
such sums as may be necessary to carry out this subsection. Amounts
appropriated under this paragraph are authorized to remain available until
expended.
(c) Waiver.—
(1) In general.—Notwithstanding any other provision of law, the Secretary of
Homeland Security shall have the authority to waive all legal requirements
such Secretary, in such Secretary’s sole discretion, determines necessary to
ensure expeditious construction of the barriers and roads under this section.
3a

Any such decision by the Secretary shall be effective upon being published in
the Federal Register.
(2) Federal court review.—
(A) In general.—The district courts of the United States shall have
exclusive jurisdiction to hear all causes or claims arising from any action
undertaken, or any decision made, by the Secretary of Homeland
Security pursuant to paragraph (1). A cause of action or claim may only
be brought alleging a violation of the Constitution of the United States.
The court shall not have jurisdiction to hear any claim not specified in
this subparagraph.
(B) Time for filing of complaint.—Any cause or claim brought pursuant
to subparagraph (A) shall be filed not later than 60 days after the date
of the action or decision made by the Secretary of Homeland Security. A
claim shall be barred unless it is filed within the time specified.
(C) Ability to seek appellate review.—An interlocutory or final
judgment, decree, or order of the district court may be reviewed only
upon petition for a writ of certiorari to the Supreme Court of the United
States.
4a

III. Summary of Public Comments
Received and Agency Response to
Comments
As indicated in Unit I.C., EPA did
receive comments in response to the
notice of receipt that published in the
Federal Register of August 5, 2025,
including comments from registrants to
withdraw their requests to cancel their
registrations. Accordingly, EPA has
removed those products from Table 3
and the company name and address
from Table 4.
IV. Provisions for Disposition of
Existing Stocks
Existing stocks are those stocks of
registered pesticide products which are
currently in the United States, and
which were packaged, labeled, and
released for shipment prior to the
effective date of the cancellation action.
The existing stocks provisions for the
products subject to this order are as
follows.
Registrants may continue to sell and
distribute existing stocks of these
products until January 15, 2026.
Thereafter, registrants will be prohibited
from selling or distributing the
pesticides identified in Tables 1 and 3
of Unit II., except for export consistent
with FIFRA section 17 or for proper
disposal. Persons other than registrants
will generally be allowed to sell,
distribute, or use existing stocks until
such stocks are exhausted, provided that
such sale, distribution, or use is
consistent with the terms of the
previously approved labeling on, or that
accompanied, the canceled products.
Authority: 7 U.S.C. 136 et seq.

DEPARTMENT OF HOMELAND

Office of the Secretary
Determination Pursuant to Section 102
of the Illegal Immigration Reform and
Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996,
as Amended
AGENCY: Office of the Secretary,
Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION: Notice of determination.
SUMMARY: The Secretary of Homeland
Security has determined, pursuant to
law, that it is necessary to waive certain
laws, regulations, and other legal
requirements in order to ensure the
expeditious construction of barriers and
roads in the vicinity of the international
border in the state of Arizona.
DATES: This determination takes effect
on October 15, 2025.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Important
mission requirements of the Department
of Homeland Security (‘‘DHS’’) include
border security and the detection and
prevention of illegal entry into the
United States. Border security is critical
to the nation’s national security.
Recognizing the critical importance of
border security, Congress has mandated
DHS to achieve and maintain
operational control of the international
border. Secure Fence Act of 2006,
Public Law 109–367, section 2, 120 Stat.
2638 (Oct. 26, 2006) (8 U.S.C. 1701
note). Congress defined ‘‘operational
control’’ as the prevention of all
unlawful entries into the United States,
including entries by terrorists, other
unlawful aliens, instruments of
terrorism, narcotics, and other
contraband. Id. Consistent with that
mandate, the President’s Executive
Order on Securing Our Borders directs
that I take all appropriate action to
deploy and construct physical barriers
to ensure complete operational control
of the southern border of the United
States. Executive Order 14165, section 3
(Jan. 20, 2025).
Congress has provided to the
Secretary of Homeland Security a
number of authorities necessary to carry
out DHS’s border security mission. One
of those authorities is found at section
102 of the Illegal Immigration Reform
and Immigrant Responsibility Act of
1996, as amended (‘‘IIRIRA’’). Public
Law 104–208, Div. C, 110 Stat. 3009–
546, 3009–554 (Sept. 30, 1996) (8 U.S.C.
1103 note), as amended by the REAL ID
Act of 2005, Public Law 109–13, Div. B,
119 Stat. 231, 302, 306 (May 11, 2005)
(8 U.S.C. 1103 note), as amended by the
Secure Fence Act of 2006, Public Law
109–367, section 3, 120 Stat. 2638 (Oct.
26, 2006) (8 U.S.C. 1103 note), as
amended by the Department of
Homeland Security Appropriations Act,
2008, Public Law 110–161, Div. E, Title
V, section 564, 121 Stat. 2090 (Dec. 26,
2007). In section 102(a) of IIRIRA,
Congress provided that the Secretary of
Homeland Security shall take such
actions as may be necessary to install
additional physical barriers and roads
(including the removal of obstacles to
detection of illegal entrants) in the
vicinity of the United States border to
deter illegal crossings in areas of high
illegal entry into the United States. In
section 102(b) of IIRIRA, Congress
mandated that in carrying out the
authority of section 102(a), I provide for
the installation of additional fencing,
barriers, roads, lighting, cameras, and
sensors to achieve and maintain
operational control of the border.
Finally, in section 102(c) of IIRIRA,
Congress granted to the Secretary of
Homeland Security the authority to
waive all legal requirements that I, in
my sole discretion, determine necessary
to ensure the expeditious construction
of barriers and roads authorized by
section 102 of IIRIRA.

2025, the United States Border Patrol
(‘‘Border Patrol’’) apprehended over
1,318,645 illegal aliens attempting to
enter the United States between border
crossings in the Tucson Sector. In that
same time period, Border Patrol seized

Since the President took office, DHS
has delivered the most secure border in

Because the Tucson Sector is an area of

States or smuggle illicit drugs, and given
my mandate to achieve and maintain

use my authority under section 102 of

DHS will take immediate action to
construct additional barriers and roads
in the Tucson Sector.
Section 2
I determine that the Tucson Sector,
which is in the vicinity of the United
States border and located in the state of
Arizona, is an area of high illegal entry.
There is presently an acute and
immediate need to construct physical
barriers and roads in the vicinity of the
border of the United States in order to
prevent unlawful entries into the United
States and achieve and maintain
operational control of the border in the
Tucson Sector pursuant to sections
102(a) and 102(b) of IIRIRA. In order to
ensure the expeditious construction of
the barriers and roads in the Tucson
Sector, I have determined that it is
necessary that I exercise the authority
that is vested in me by section 102(c) of
IIRIRA. Accordingly, pursuant to
section 102(c) of IIRIRA, I hereby waive
with respect to all contracting actions
necessary for the construction of
physical barriers and roads (including,
but not limited to, accessing the project
areas, creating and using staging areas,
the conduct of earthwork, excavation,
fill, and site preparation, and
installation and upkeep of physical
barriers, roads, supporting elements,
drainage, erosion controls, safety
features, lighting, cameras, and sensors)
in the Tucson Sector, all of the
following statutes and regulations,
including any legal requirements of,
deriving from, or related to the subject
of, the following statutes and
regulations: the Administrative
Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. 551, et seq.); 15
U.S.C. 63l(j); 15 U.S.C. 637(d)–(f), and
(h)–(k); 15 U.S.C. 644; 15 U.S.C. 657q;
28 U.S.C. 1491(b) (to the extent that it
authorizes injunctive relief or any form
thereof that would interfere with the
expeditious construction of barriers and
roads); 31 U.S.C. 3553(c) and (d)(3); 40
U.S.C. 1101 et seq.; 41 U.S.C. 1126; 41
U.S.C. 1708(a), (c), (e)–(g); 41 U.S.C.
1901(c), (d), and (e); 41 U.S.C. 3301; 41
U.S.C. 3302(b)–(e); 41 U.S.C. 3304; 41
U.S.C. 3306(a)–(c); 41 U.S.C. 3307(b)–
(d), (e)(4), and (e)(5)(C); 41 U.S.C. 3309;
41 U.S.C. 3502; Section 880 of Division
A, Title VIII of Public Law 115–232 (41
U.S.C. 3701, Note); 41 U.S.C. 4103(c),
(d)(3)–(4); 41 U.S.C. 4104(b); 41 U.S.C.
4105(c)–(d), (f)(2)–(3), (g); 41 U.S.C.
4106(c)–(d); 41 U.S.C. 6101(b)(1); 13
CFR part 125, and 127.503(g); 48 CFR
7.102; 48 CFR part 10; 48 CFR 16.504(c);
48 CFR 16.505(a)(4), (a)(8)(i) and (iii),
(a)(9), and (b); 48 CFR 17.207; 48 CFR
22.404–5; 48 CFR subpart 22.5; 48 CFR
28.102–1(c); 48 CFR 33.103(f).
This waiver does not revoke or
supersede any other waiver
determination made pursuant to section
102(c) of IIRIRA. Such waivers shall
remain in full force and effect in
accordance with their terms. I reserve
the authority to execute further waivers
from time to time as I may determine to
be necessary under section 102 of
IIRIRA.
Kristi Noem,
Secretary of Homeland Security.

Section 1
The United States Border Patrol Big
Bend Sector is an area of high illegal
entry. Between fiscal year 2021 and July
2025, the United States Border Patrol
(‘‘Border Patrol’’) apprehended over
88,595 illegal aliens attempting to enter
the United States between border
crossings in the Big Bend Sector. In that
same time period, Border Patrol seized
over 86,851 pounds of marijuana, over
863 pounds of cocaine, over 12 pounds
of heroin, over 1,084 pounds of
methamphetamine, and over 94 pounds
of fentanyl.
Since the President took office, DHS
has delivered the most secure border in
history. More can be done, however.
Because the Big Bend Sector is an area
of high illegal entry where illegal aliens
regularly attempt to enter the United

my mandate to achieve and maintain
operational control of the border, I must
use my authority under section 102 of
IIRIRA to install additional barriers and
roads in the Big Bend Sector. Therefore,
DHS will take immediate action to
construct additional barriers and roads
in the Big Bend Sector.

out DHS’s border security mission. One

amended by the Department of
Homeland Security Appropriations Act,
2008, Public Law 110–161, Div. E, Title
V, section 564, 121 Stat. 2090 (Dec. 26,
2007). In section 102(a) of IIRIRA,
Congress provided that the Secretary of
Homeland Security shall take such
actions as may be necessary to install
additional physical barriers and roads
(including the removal of obstacles to
detection of illegal entrants) in the
vicinity of the United States border to
deter illegal crossings in areas of high
illegal entry into the United States. In
section 102(b) of IIRIRA, Congress
mandated that in carrying out the
authority of section 102(a), I provide for
the installation of additional fencing,
barriers, roads, lighting, cameras, and
sensors to achieve and maintain
operational control of the border.
Finally, in section 102(c) of IIRIRA,
Congress granted to the Secretary of
Homeland Security the authority to
waive all legal requirements that I, in
my sole discretion, determine necessary
to ensure the expeditious construction
of barriers and roads authorized by
section 102 of IIRIRA.
Determination and Waiver
Section 1
The United States Border Patrol San
Diego Sector is an area of high illegal
entry. Between fiscal year 2021 and July
2025, the United States Border Patrol

922,000 illegal aliens attempting to
enter the United States between border
crossings in the San Diego Sector. In
that same time period, Border Patrol
seized over 2,465 pounds of marijuana,
over 9,873 pounds of cocaine, over 565
pounds of heroin, over 29,675 pounds of
methamphetamine, and over 4,016
pounds of fentanyl.

has delivered the most secure border in
history. More can be done, however.
Because the San Diego Sector is an area
of high illegal entry where illegal aliens
regularly attempt to enter the United

my mandate to achieve and maintain
operational control of the border, I must
use my authority under section 102 of
IIRIRA to install additional barriers and
roads in the San Diego Sector.

action to construct additional barriers
and roads in the San Diego Sector.

INTRODUCTION
Colorful immensity and primeval magnificence fill the beholder with a great sense
of upheaval, a feeling that gods older than ours clapped their hands to command
the canyons into sudden glorious being. The pedestrian mind of man is linked for
an instant with the force that created man and mountain. Up among the craggy

roughhouse that gouges and rends chasms through the heart of the mountains . . .
No man has altered that country, but it has altered many a man.
Mary Lasswell, Coloraturas in the Canyon (1958).
1.
In this action, Plaintiffs challenge the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s
(“DHS” or “the Agency”) unconstitutional repeal of bedrock environmental and historic
protections and dozens of other federal laws to expedite massive border wall construction on the
Texas-Mexico border that will destroy iconic sections of the Rio Grande corridor in the United
States while tarnishing the carefully wrought web of laws meant to protect a vast universe of
biological, historic, cultural, and other interests.
2.
Texas’s far west region is called the “Big Bend” because it encompasses the Rio
Grande’s south and then northward curvature around the Chisos mountains. The river corridor is
life-sustaining for an extraordinarily diverse range of rare and endemic plants and animals in the
Chihuahuan Desert, houses abundant archeological, cultural, and historic resources, and boasts
some of the darkest skies in the continental U.S. Mammals such as the pronghorn, black bear,
javelina, bighorn sheep, and a unique type of whitetail deer, the Carmen Mountain deer, roam this
region.
3.
On February 17, June 9, and July 27, 2026, the Secretary of Homeland Security
announced that the Agency will construct “additional barriers and roads” in the Big Bend region:
one project area spans over 250 miles along the Rio Grande (“West Wall Project”), the second
project area encompasses Big Bend National Park and covers an additional 180 miles of border

The Chihuahuan Desert is the largest desert in North America and one of the most
biologically diverse desert ecosystems on the planet. The Rio Grande, called the Rio Bravo in
Mexico, is the primary major river flowing through the Chihuahuan Desert and is the main artery
of the Big Bend region. This area boasts extraordinary geology, biology, and history, and lies at
the confluence of multiple major ecosystems, including desert grasslands, limestone canyons, sky
islands, and riparian corridors.

LEGAL BACKGROUND
A.
The Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996
31.
Congress initially enacted IIRIRA in 1996 to, for the first time, provide federal

agencies with specific direction regarding the location and extent of border barriers to be
constructed. P.L. 104-208, div. C., codified at 8 U.S.C. § 1103 note. Prior to IIRIRA, the authority
to construct border barriers derived from the general statutory responsibility of the Attorney
General (now the DHS Secretary) to “guard the boundaries and borders of the United States against
the illegal entry of aliens.” Immigration and Nationality Act, § 103(a)(5), 8 U.S.C. § 1103(a)(5).
That authority continues to exist independent of IIRIRA.
32.
While it has been amended several times, IIRIRA Section 102 remains the primary
federal statutory provision addressing border barriers. Section 102(a) remains substantively the
same as originally enacted in 1996, providing the U.S. Attorney General (now the DHS Secretary)
with the general policy direction to “take such actions as may be necessary to install additional
physical barriers and roads . . . in the vicinity of the United States border to deter illegal crossings
in areas of high illegal entry into the United States.”
33.
At the time Section 102(a) was enacted, Congress also provided that “to the extent
the Attorney General determines necessary to ensure expeditious construction of the barriers and
roads under this Section,” the specific requirements of the ESA and NEPA may be waived.
34.
As originally enacted, IIRIRA Section 102(b) “carr[ied] out subsection (a)” by
identifying specific border barriers to be constructed, establishing specific deadlines for the
construction of such barriers, and other requirements. The only border fence segment initially
mandated by Congress under IIRIRA Section 102(b) was the construction of 14 miles of fencing
in San Diego, California.

The major questions doctrine demands a clear congressional statement before an
executive body may assert authority over “decisions of vast economic and political significance.”
West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697, 716 (2022) (cleaned up) (quoting Utility Air Regulatory

legislative power to Congress by counseling skepticism where an agency claims sweeping
authority absent unmistakably clear text.

The Constitution provides that “[a]ll legislative Powers herein granted shall be
vested in a Congress of the United States,” U.S. Const. art. 1, § 1, thereby forming “a separation
of powers between the legislative and executive branches that the Framers viewed as essential to
the preservation of individual liberty.” V.O.S. Selections, Inc. v. United States, 772 F. Supp. 3d
1350, 1371 (Ct. Int’l Trade 2025) (citing The Federalist No. 48 (James Madison)). Thus, where
“[t]he Constitution lodges the Nation’s lawmaking powers in Congress alone . . . the major
questions doctrine safeguards that assignment against executive encroachment.” Learning Res.,
Inc. v. Trump, Nos. 24-1287, 25-250, 146 S. Ct. 628, 646 (Feb. 20, 2026) (Gorsuch, J., concurring).

the Rio Grande. Such state-created entitlements to navigable waters are held in trust for the public.
See Ill. C. R. Co. v. Illinois, 146 U.S. 387, 455 (1892) (“property is held by the State, by virtue of
its sovereignty, in trust for the public. The ownership of the navigable waters . . . is a subject of
public concern to the whole people of the State.”); Tex. Const. Art. XVI, § 59 (“The conservation
and development of all of the natural resources of this State . . . the waters of its rivers and streams
. . . the navigation of its inland and coastal waters, and the preservation and conservation of all
such natural resources of the State are each and all hereby declared public rights and duties.”);
State v. Bradford, 50 S.W.2d 1065, 1069 (Tex. 1932) (“From its earliest history this state has
announced its public policy that lands underlying navigable waters are held in trust for the use and
benefit of the public.”). Additionally, Plaintiff Miller maintains ongoing personal and established
commercial interests in using the Rio Grande as a commercial river guide whose work depends on

FIFTH CLAIM FOR RELIEF
Violation of the Presentment Clause
Article I, Section 7 of the U.S. Constitution
108.
The preceding paragraphs are incorporated herein by reference.
109.
Article I, § 7 of the Constitution provides that any federal statute must pass both
houses of Congress, and “before it become a Law, be presented to the President of the United
States: If he[/she] approve he shall sign it, but if not he shall return it, with his Objections to that
House it which it shall have originated, who shall enter the Objections at large on their Journal,
and proceed to reconsider it.”
110.
The “[a]mendment and repeal of statutes, no less than enactment,” must conform
with the presentment and bicameralism requirements of Article I.  INS v. Chadha, 462 U.S. 919,
954 (1983). Specifically, the Supreme Court has stated that the Executive Branch cannot void any
law without Congress passing a law voiding the previous law and presenting it to the President for
signature. Clinton v. City of New York, 524 U.S. 417 (1998).
111.
IIRIRA Section 102(c), as written, is facially invalid because it vests unilateral
power in the DHS Secretary to, in effect, repeal portions of duly-enacted statutes via its delegation
of waiver authority in areas along the border for purpose of border construction without Congress
passing a law to void or amend the specific laws at issue or limit their application, and presenting
it to the President, as required by Article I, Section 7 of the U.S. Constitution.
112.
Separately, the statute is also invalid as applied to this case. The National Park and
Lower Canyons Waivers purport to waive the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act and numerous other
laws that would otherwise apply to the Big Bend Wall Project at issue in this litigation. In so doing,
the Secretary unilaterally repealed legal protections provided by statute for certain Congressionally

67a

46
designated areas. For example, the National Park and Lower Canyons Waivers remove legal
protections provided under the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act for a segment of the Rio Grande
specifically designated for such protections by Congress. See 16 U.S.C. § 1274(a)(17) (designating
the segment of the Rio Grande in Texas “on the United States side of the river from river mile
842.3 above Mariscal Canyon downstream to river mile 651.1 at the Terrell-Val Verde County
line” as a “component[] of the national wild and scenic river system”); see also id. §§ 1271(b)
(declaring the national policy that “certain selected rivers” and their immediate environments that
“possess outstandingly remarkable scenic, recreational, geologic, fish and wildlife, historic,
cultural, or other similar values” be preserved in free-flowing condition and that they be protected
for the benefit and enjoyment of present and future generations), 1281(a) (mandating that
responsible agencies administer components of the national wild and scenic rivers system “in such
a manner as to protect and enhance the values which caused it to be included in said system . . .
.”). The Secretary’s waiver of the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act for the construction of border
barriers and roads in the vicinity of this Congressionally-protected segment of the Rio Grande
would degrade or destroy the scenic, geologic, fish and wildlife, and recreational values that make
the area eligible for inclusion as part of the wild and scenic river system, and thus preclude the
responsible agency—here, the National Park Service—from administering the area in a manner
that would protect and enhance these values. Once the values that make this specified portion of
the Rio Grande eligible for inclusion and serve as the basis for protection as a component of the
wild and scenic river system are permanently diminished or destroyed by such construction, the
statute no longer has the same legal effect as when it was enacted by Congress. In other words,
through the National Park and Lower Canyons Waivers, the Secretary struck the portion of the
Wild and Scenic Rivers Act designating this specific area for its “outstandingly remarkable” values

General Management Plan / Environmental Impact Statement
RIO GRANDE WILD AND SCENIC RIVER
Brewster and Terrell Counties, Texas
August 2004
Congress designated a segment of the Rio Grande
in Texas as the Rio Grande Wild and Scenic River
in 1978 because of its “outstandingly remarkable”
scenic, geologic, fish and wildlife, and recreational
values. A 196-mile strip of land on the American
side of the Rio Grande in the Chihuahuan Desert
protects the river. The National Park Service (NPS)
at Big Bend National Park is responsible for man-
aging the wild and scenic river. This General Man-
agement Plan / Environmental Impact Statement will
define a direction for the management of the Rio
Grande Wild and Scenic River for the next 15 to 20
years, specifying the resource conditions and visi-
tor experiences that the National Park Service
would like to achieve.
To establish the desired experiences and resource
conditions for the wild and scenic river, a partner-
ship team was established with representatives
from Texas Parks and Wildlife, local counties, an
international environmental organization, river
user groups, and private landowners. On the basis
of public comments and within the framework es-
tablished by legislation and mandates, the planning
team and partners developed a no-action alterna-
tive (continuation of current management) and an
“action” alternative for managing the wild and
scenic river.
Alternative A, the no-action alternative, would
continue current management practices into the
future. Its goal would be to retain the existing
visitor experiences. No new management plan
would be implemented. The National Park Service
would respond to future needs and conditions
associated with the existing wild and scenic river
designation without major actions or changes in
course. Compliance with the Wild and Scenic
Rivers Act and associated guidelines requires a
river management plan, which would not be
prepared under this alternative. No agreements
with landowners would be initiated, and there
would be no changes in river access from federal
land. Private and state landowners could open or
close public access as they wished. The river
boundary would remain at the default 0.25 mile
from the ordinary high water mark on the United
States side of the river.
The intent of Alternative B, the preferred alter-
native, would be to enhance resource protection
and offer high-quality visitor experiences. The pro-
tection of natural and cultural resources would be
emphasized, as would the visitor experience. A
permanent boundary for the wild and scenic river
would be established to reflect the river’s outstand-
ingly remarkable values. The National Park Service
would negotiate individual agreements with each
nonfederal landowner to specify the rights and re-
sponsibilities of the National Park Service and each
landowner. The National Park Service would rec-
ommend to Congress that the upper segment of the
Rio Grande in Big Bend National Park be desig-
nated a wild and scenic river, bringing the total
federal and state ownership along the river to more
than 50%.
Alternative A (which would continue the manage-
ment pattern of the past 25 years) would not ensure
the protection of outstandingly remarkable values
on private lands. It would mean that no partnership
for resource protection would be established be-
tween the National Park Service and private land-
owners. Resources could be damaged, and private
lands now available to the public for recreational
use at the sufferance of landowners could be closed
off. The National Park Service would not assist pri-
vate landowners in resource protection or law
enforcement, and there could be continued mis-
trust of NPS intentions with respect to regulations
and land acquisition.
Landowner agreements in alternative B would
foster a cooperative relationship, allowing the
National Park Service to play a role in protecting
resources and values on nonfederal lands. NPS
assistance would be available to landowners to
protect outstandingly remarkable values on their
land. An increase in Big Bend National Park staff
would be included in this alternative. Beneficial
effects on landowner relations, natural resources,
cultural resources, scenic values, and recreational
use would result from alternative B.

river. Few clients undertake the remarkable 84-mile journey through the Lower Canyons because
the trip is demanding and often takes more than a week by boat. Those who do make the journey,
however, are rewarded with some of the clearest spring-fed waters and most dramatic canyon
scenery in the Big Bend region. What makes the Lower Canyons especially meaningful to me is
its remoteness. It remains one of the few places where a person can spend days on the river
immersed in the landscape, seeing little evidence of modern development and experiencing the

DECLARATION OF WILLARD “BILL” GUERRA-ADDINGTON IN

I, Willard Guerra-Addington, declare as follows:
1.
This declaration is based on my personal knowledge. If called as a witness in this
proceeding, I could and would competently testify to the facts stated below.
2.
I have been a supporter of the Center for Biological Diversity since 2018 and
became a member in 2026. The organization is one of the few groups that I believe truly works to
protect my interests in species and habitat protection—especially in the borderlands.
3.
I have lived and worked in the greater Big Bend region of Texas for most of my
life. I am a third-generation rancher and farmer in southern Hudspeth County. In 1915, my
grandfather immigrated from Merida, Yucatán to Galveston, Texas on a U.S. Naval ship. He
walked with other immigrants from Galveston to Valentine, Texas, where he met my grandmother,
who was visiting her brother, the owner of a big hardware store in Valentine, Texas, a thriving
steam railroad water stop community 40 miles from Sierra Blanca. They fell in love and married
in Valentine. Seeing opportunity, my grandparents moved to Sierra Blanca and built an Adobe
Case 3:26-cv-01099-KC     Document 55-1     Filed 09/19/26     Page 1 of 9
142a

2
home. My grandfather borrowed money from a good friend in El Paso and sold goods delivered
by mules and a wagon down a dirt road to small communities and railroad camps on the Southern
Pacific Railroad. The wagon trip was 170 miles to Sanderson, Texas. He built a small Adobe
grocery and general store south of the railroad tracks which was known as the “Mexican Town”
or Pueblo Mexicano in Sierra Blanca. In 1926, they built a much larger general store and
lumberyard in downtown Sierra Blanca when Highway 80 was constructed through Sierra Blanca.
Years later, after expanding the general store and finding success, my grandfather, purchased a
large ranch (100 sections, or 100 square miles) and also purchased river and ranch lands on the
Rio Grande.
4.
I was born in Fort Hancock 30 miles from Sierra Blanca. As a young boy, I worked
my family’s ranch for years into adulthood. Our ranch consistently had at least 300 head of cattle
and grew alfalfa, pecans, watermelons and Pima cotton. Today, I reside in my Sierra Blanca rock
home, in a house my grandfather built in 1928. I am very proud of my heritage and the hard work,
sweat and blood my grandfather put into these lands.
5.
Today, I own my family’s land, called Guerra Farm and Ranch. This property abuts
the Rio Grande and U.S.-Mexico border. It falls within the pathway of the planned border wall
construction for Big Bend Project 1 and is encompassed by waivers issued by the Secretary of
Homeland Security (91 Fed. Reg. 7297 (Feb. 17, 2026), as amended by 91 Fed. Reg. 40550 (July
2, 2026), referred to in this case as the “West Waiver”). Customs and Border Protection’s online
plans for this area show 30-foot-tall steel bollard walls along the entirety of my property. I would
lose hundreds of acres to border wall construction if it is completed.
6.
Words barely scratch the surface of the great love and connection I have and feel
for this region and my deeply held historic, aesthetic, recreational, scientific, and spiritual interests
Case 3:26-cv-01099-KC     Document 55-1     Filed 09/19/26     Page 2 of 9
143a

3
on my land and all of the Rio Grande borderlands. I know I can’t protect the whole river, but I’ll
do my best to protect this stretch of it in southern Hudspeth County because it has given so much
to my family and myself since 1918. The Guerra Farm and Ranch and the vast unspoiled
undeveloped greater Big Bend region is a part of me.
7.
The Rio Grande does not flow like it used to through this region—but it still brings
life-sustaining water to the land, wildlife, and ecosystem. The dramatic landscape is covered with
mesquite, creosote, catclaw, ocotillo, great yucca dagger “forests,” and many species of cactus.
The greater Big Bend region, part of the Chihuahuan Desert, is said to be as biodiverse as the
Amazon rainforest. The greater Big Bend region has the darkest sky I’ve ever seen. Since I was a
child, I have spent countless nights gazing for hours at the dark sky, sleeping under countless stars.
I have slept outside, one with this sacred land, more nights than I have under a roof. The roots of
my spirituality flow through this region—it is my home, it is embedded in my spirit. The great
mountains, the gentle hills, and the life-sustaining river are my church and Cathedral where I
worship God and creation. The Rio Grande and the great Eagle and Indio Mountains, where a
portion of my ranch resides, are the most beautiful and sacred living things to me. A 30-foot steel
bollard wall with patrol roads and stadium lighting would cause me great damage and insult, and
degrade my ranch and farm and the entire Rio Grande region. I probably would not be able to ever
grow crops again after being cut off from the Rio Grande waters. The nights would never be as
dark. And the natural wildlife and habitats of this region would be severed.
8.
My interests in the species here are aesthetic, scientific, and spiritual. On and
around my ranch, I have lived with and seen mule deer, javelina, skunks, Mexican freetail bats,
mountain lions, bobcats, foxes, porcupines, river beavers, and countless other wild animals.
Threatened species like the Texas horned lizard live on my farm, as do the most beautiful Night
Case 3:26-cv-01099-KC     Document 55-1     Filed 09/19/26     Page 3 of 9
144a

4
Blooming Cereus cactus. Three weeks ago, in mid-August 2026, for the first time, I was amazed
to see and hear a large black bear walking not far from my farmhouse at night. Seeing these wild
animals live and roam the lands I love so much fills me with profound joy. Bears are coming back
to their home immigrating from Mexico, on our ranch and throughout the greater Big Bend region.
A wall would stop black bear’s re-introduction to Big Bend and would also stop their back-and-
forth movements, necessary to find food and mate, thereby weakening their genetic pool. The Rio
Grande often serves as the sole source of drinking water for animals in this region, wild and
domestic. Wild animals will walk for many miles to the Rio Grande to find and drink water. I pray
to God every night and every morning when I awake that this violent outrage on my ranch, farm
and Rio Grande region will not happen.
9.
I visit and work at my ranch around 3-5 times or more per week. I tend to and work
on my land, enjoying the majestic scenery and beauty of the land and wildlife, while I still can. I
take long hikes, ride my horse Escondido for miles, and check on the cattle and burros living on
our farm. When I spend the night, I sit and lay on a cot around a Mesquite campfire, and gaze at
the stars in our beautiful dark sky. I do this for hours, until I fall asleep. I prefer to sleep outside
instead of in the farmhouse unless it’s very cold in the winter. In the daytime, you can clearly see
for 70 miles or more in many places. The beautiful feeling of living in the moment in quiet space
and time cannot be put into words. My ranch and farm and all of the greater Big Bend region is
the last virtually wild and undeveloped region in Texas. This region is a treasure to Texas and our
great nation. It is sacred to me. Witnessing some of this beautiful borderland degraded and
destroyed has caused me great sadness, grief and trauma. I’m not sure if I could ever begin to

on the border frontier, I am deeply connected and part of this land. Any living being including

 I also have historic interests in preserving and maintaining my property because it

site on September 4, 7, and 9, 2026 and observed great amounts of dust clouds and smoke billowing
from disparate corners of the massive clearing, approximately 50 industrial vehicles, many

On September 4, 2026 I travelled past my ranch, past the Barnard staging area, to

I, Robert J.  Krumenaker, declare as follows:
1. This declaration is based on my personal knowledge. If called as a witness in this
proceeding, I could and would competently testify to the facts stated below.
2. I serve as Chair of Keep Big Bend Wild, a citizen initiative dedicated to protecting the
wilderness character of Big Bend National Park. Keep Big Bend Wild and another non-profit
organization, The Coalition to Protect America’s National Parks, filed an amicus brief in this case
on August 14, 2026. ECF No. 19-1. I make this declaration in my individual capacity, not on behalf
of either amicus organization.
3. Prior to my retirement, I served as Superintendent of Big Bend National Park and the
Rio Grande Wild and Scenic River from September 2018 through July 2023. I submit this
declaration based on my personal knowledge and experience as a former Superintendent.
4. As Superintendent, I was the senior National Park Service official responsible for the
management and operation of Big Bend National Park and the Rio Grande Wild and Scenic River.
My role encompassed law enforcement operations, natural and cultural resource management,
Case 3:26-cv-01099-KC     Document 55-4     Filed 09/19/26     Page 1 of 15
152a

2

visitor services, budgeting, personnel, and coordination with federal, local, and international
partners.
5. The areas under my supervision included approximately 245 miles of the international
border with Mexico, from the upstream boundary of Big Bend National Park at approximately
river mile 902.2, just below the village of Lajitas, TX, to the downstream boundary of the Rio
Grande Wild & Scenic River, at approximately river mile 657.5 at the Terrell – Val Verde (TX)
County line, which amounts to approximately 12.5% of the entire U.S.-Mexico border.
6. During my tenure, border security in the Big Bend region functioned through
cooperation among the Border Patrol, National Park Service, and county sheriffs rather than
through extensive physical infrastructure.
7. As Superintendent, I was part of that collaborative effort to promote border security. I
worked closely with U.S. Border Patrol and other law enforcement agencies. I regularly met with
Border Patrol leadership and participated in efforts to coordinate National Park Service and Border
Patrol activities within the region. Additionally, I started a record system that tracked the annual
number of apprehensions for unauthorized crossings within Big Bend National Park. The data was
provided to the National Park Service by Border Patrol agents stationed in the park and compiled
in an Excel sheet.
8. The National Park Service maintained up to eighteen to twenty commissioned law
enforcement rangers within the area during my tenure. Although National Park Service rangers
were not responsible for enforcing federal immigration laws, they frequently coordinated with
Border Patrol personnel and often served as first responders when activity was detected in remote
portions of the park.
Case 3:26-cv-01099-KC     Document 55-4     Filed 09/19/26     Page 2 of 15
153a

9. During my tenure, there were no human-made border barriers of any kind within Big
Bend National Park or along the Rio Grande Wild and Scenic River. Instead, border enforcement
relied on personnel, patrols, aircraft, remote sensors, intelligence, and interagency coordination.
Wireless remote sensors were deployed throughout the region. In my experience, these systems
were effective, inexpensive, and adaptable. Sensor alerts were shared among agencies, allowing
personnel to respond quickly when activity was detected.
10.
The National Park Service also operated aerial patrols, and the Border Patrol
regularly conducted aerial surveillance throughout the region.
11.
Throughout my service as Superintendent, Border Patrol leadership never indicated
that existing security operations within the park were inadequate or that substantially different
enforcement mechanisms were necessary.
12.
Based on my experience, the combination of terrain, surveillance technology, law
enforcement personnel, and interagency cooperation was effective in supporting border
enforcement operations in Big Bend National Park.
13.
I am very familiar with the geography and terrain of Big Bend National Park and
the adjacent region in Mexico.
14.
Big Bend National Park is naturally isolated by surrounding deserts, canyons, and
mountains. In my experience, these geographic features function as substantial natural barriers to
travel. Big Bend is a desert environment characterized by extreme remoteness, steep mountains,
deep canyons, rugged desert terrain, dense riparian vegetation along portions of the Rio Grande,
substantial elevation changes, limited water sources, and extreme temperatures.
15.
The highest point within the park exceeds 7,800 feet in elevation, more than a mile
above the Rio Grande. The lowest point is where the Rio Grande exits the park at approximately
Case 3:26-cv-01099-KC     Document 55-4     Filed 09/19/26     Page 3 of 15
154a

4

1,800 feet. Many areas contain steep slopes, rugged canyon systems, and sharp vegetation that is
difficult to traverse. Travel through much of the region is slow, difficult, and potentially dangerous.
Most areas lack readily available water. Summer temperatures commonly exceed 110 degrees
Fahrenheit near the border. The landscape also contains numerous natural hazards, including steep
terrain, thorny vegetation, venomous wildlife, and other environmental dangers.
16.
I have visited the region across the international border in Mexico on numerous
occasions. In my experience, the terrain on the Mexican side of the border is similarly remote,
rugged, and difficult to traverse.
17.
The rugged terrain, natural barriers, isolation, and distance from major
transportation routes are principal reasons why the Big Bend region experiences low levels of
illegal crossing activity. In my experience, of those who did migrate through this region, many of
them sought humanitarian assistance or medical aid due to the arduous journey through the
landscape.
18.
I prepared the table attached hereto as Exhibit 1, titled “Illegal Migrant Activity in
Big Bend National Park.”
19.
The figures contained in that table were derived from publicly available Customs
and Border Protection data and information provided to the National Park Service by the Border
Patrol and later produced by the National Park Service in response to a Freedom of Information
Act request I filed on May 27, 2026 (the “FOIA Request”).
20.
The apprehension figures reflected in Exhibit 1 demonstrate that Big Bend National
Park accounts for a very small proportion of activity along the southern border. For example, in
both 2023 and 2024, the park accounted 0.005% of all unauthorized crossing apprehensions along
the southern border. To illustrate how remarkably small this number is in relation to the park’s

expansive geography, there were just 0.092 apprehensions per mile per month along the park’s
118-mile border in 2023. In 2024, this number dropped to 0.072 apprehensions per mile per month
of the park’s border.
21.
With the exception of figures from 2025, the figures produced in response to my
FOIA Request largely match those I compiled as Superintendent during the years of my tenure.
The 2025 figures are an outlier. In response to my FOIA Request, the National Park Service
produced two documents. Attached hereto as Exhibit 2 are true and correct copies of records
produced by the National Park Service in response to my FOIA Request. One reflected an annual
total of 613 Ü°°£êìêü§î†üs for 2025. The second contained monthly figures that did not correspond
to that annual total and appeared to inconsistently report different categories of activity,
including encounters and individuals who were not formally apprehended but returned to their
country of origin shortly after crossing the border. Much of the data in that second document
included activity that did not take place inside the National Park, which was the intended scope of
the FOIA Request. When I totaled the monthly figures of just the apprehensions inside the
national park, reflected in that document, the sum was 123, which is substantially lower than the
613 reported. The 123 figure is more consistent with my understanding of conditions in the park.
22.
The very qualities that make Big Bend National Park remote and difficult to
traverse are also central to its significance as a national park and the visitor experience. One of the
defining characteristics of Big Bend National Park is its sense of remoteness, wildness, open space,
and lack of visible human development away from the existing roads. During my service as
Superintendent, visitors routinely expressed appreciation for the park’s undeveloped character,
expansive vistas, wildlife, solitude, and exceptionally dark night skies. Many visitors traveled long

156a

distances to experience this, and the communities neighboring the National Park have shaped their
businesses and operations around this tourism.
23.
Proposed construction of additional border infrastructure could involve barriers,
roads, lighting, cameras, fixed sensors on poles or towers, communications and power lines and
related infrastructure, staging areas, man camps, wells, excavation, grading, and related operations
and facilities. Such development would alter portions of the landscape that currently retain a
largely undeveloped and wilderness character.
24.
Based on my observations and experience managing the park, the sense of wildness
and the opportunities for solitude a short distance from the existing park infrastructure are
significant aspects of what makes Big Bend National Park such an iconic and loved destination for
Americans that visit the park.  New roads and associated infrastructure in currently undeveloped
areas would create lasting visual impacts, fragment otherwise intact landscapes, and diminish
visitors’ ability to experience the park’s natural and wilderness qualities. Human-made
infrastructure, including roads and vehicle barriers, fragment the expansive wilderness that visitors
are aesthetically drawn to. Additionally, visible surveillance equipment makes lawful visitors
uneasy, and the feeling of being watched detracts from a sense of being immersed in nature,
replacing it with self-consciousness. Vehicle barriers would prevent recreational visitors and
outfitters from being able to back their trailers carrying canoes and other boats up to the river’s
edge, reducing or eliminating recreational opportunities.
25.
Many of the same border-security objectives currently achieved through remote,
wireless sensors and coordinated law-enforcement operations can be accomplished without the
construction of extensive, permanent infrastructure within the park.

SUPPLEMENTAL EXPERT REPORT OF ADAM B. ISACSON
1.
I am the Director for Defense Oversight at the Washington Office on Latin America
(“WOLA”), a nonprofit research and advocacy organization based in Washington, D.C.,
committed to advancing human rights in the Americas. Since 2011, a significant part of my work
has been focused on border security in the United States. I have visited the U.S.-Mexico border
approximately 40 times and the Mexico-Guatemala border 4 times. Since 2020 alone, I have
overseen WOLA’s publication of over 110 reports, memos, and multimedia projects about border
and migration trends, the successes and failures of border security and migration policies, and
human rights impacts. In addition to those products, since September 2020, I have published a
Border Update with over 500 email subscribers and more than 400,000 downloads over the past
year. I have testified about border and migration issues in the U.S. Congress three times since
November 2023. My professional opinions and work product are cited in major media outlets, on
average, a few times monthly.

ASSIGNMENT
2.
I was retained by counsel for Center for Biological Diversity (the “Center”) to opine
on the number of unlawful border crossings in the Big Bend Border Patrol Sector in Texas (the
“Big Bend Sector”); to compare those figures with unlawful border crossing data from other U.S.
Border Patrol sectors along the U.S.-Mexico border; and to determine whether the Big Bend
Sector, or any subdivision thereof, reflect comparatively elevated unlawful-entry activity.
3.
I previously submitted an expert report for this lawsuit that detailed my opinions
on this matter, ECF No. 19-2 (APX-V1-328) (“First Report” or “First Isacson Report”).
4.
Counsel for the Center requested that I provide additional context in support of my
overall conclusion that the Big Bend Sector is not an area of high illegal entry. Specifically,
Counsel for the Center asked that I break down annual entries by sector and provide additional
details to characterize the overall apprehension counts provided by Customs and Border Protection
(“CBP”).
5.
I have declined to be compensated for my time.

QUALIFICATIONS
7.

SUMMARY OF OPINIONS
8.
Review of these additional documents further supports my conclusion that the Big
Bend Sector is not an area of high illegal entry. Looking at disaggregated statistics of Border Patrol
apprehensions in this and other border sectors, as I did in my First Report, already shows that
illegal entries are extremely infrequent in the Big Bend Sector, far fewer than any other U.S.-
Mexico border sector. The number falls still further, however, when we subtract people who had
crossed the border long ago, perhaps in other sectors, only to be apprehended at vehicle
checkpoints or while otherwise “at large” in a sector that covers more than 135,000 square miles.

METHODOLOGY
9.
In order to further support my conclusion that the Big Bend Sector is not an area of
high illegal entry, I examined annual apprehension figures for all border patrol sectors per border
mile per month for every year since 1996. This data is noted in paragraph 4 of my First Report.
10.
In order to better characterize individual apprehensions within the Big Bend Sector,
I relied on annual CBP files offering further details about each individual encountered
(apprehended) by Border Patrol, as well as “at large” apprehension statistics from CBP. This data
is noted in the “Documents Reviewed” section above.
11.
 Data with details about individuals apprehended by Border Patrol are available in
a series of Excel spreadsheets, often with hundreds of thousands of rows of data: one row for each
apprehended individual. Columns provide significant detail about each apprehended individual,
including—for the purposes of this analysis—in which Border Patrol sector the apprehension
occurred, whether it occurred at a Border Patrol highway checkpoint, and how long the individual
had been present in the United States before apprehension. I used Python scripts to aggregate these
spreadsheets’ contents into a database (using SQLite), and then to query that database to determine
how many Big Bend Sector apprehensions took place at checkpoints, and of those apprehended at
checkpoints, how long they had been in the United States. I compared the Big Bend apprehension
totals to those reported by CBP over the years and presented in my First Report: during most years
from 2010-2025 they matched exactly, though there was minor variation in 2020 (total
apprehensions 0.01% lower in the spreadsheet), 2021 (total apprehensions 0.1% higher in the
spreadsheet), 2022 (total apprehensions 0.2% higher in the spreadsheet), and 2023 (total
apprehensions 0.1% higher in the spreadsheet). These very slight variances, which I confirmed by
manually inspecting the spreadsheets, likely owed to Border Patrol’s data challenges when

OPINION
13.
In my First Report, I concluded that although the Big Bend Sector encompasses
nearly one-quarter of the U.S.-Mexico border, it has the lowest rates of illegal entry. First Isacson
Decl. ¶¶ 21, 27. There, I provided two figures that illustrate how low apprehensions are in the Big
Bend Sector: Figure 1 (depicting total apprehensions per sector over various spans of years, plus
totals per mile per month for each sector), and Figure 2 (depicting a graph of total apprehensions
at the U.S.-Mexico border with the Big Bend Sector representing a nearly invisible proportion of
the total). Id. at 9.
14.
To better contextualize these figures, attached hereto as Exhibit 1 are true and
correct copies of tables I created for each year, beginning in 1996, depicting the total land border
miles for each U.S. Border Patrol sector along the U.S.-Mexico border, total apprehensions for
each sector, corresponding totals per mile per month, and overall percentages. For each year, I also
provide a pie chart showing the Big Bend Sector’s share of apprehensions.

6
15.
The annual tables show that in every year since 1996, total apprehensions per mile
per month in the Big Bend Sector have not exceeded 6, and in most years are below 2, often below
1. Other sectors see hundreds of apprehensions per mile per month.
16.
The year 1996 is a relevant starting point for this data because that was the year
Congress passed the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (“IIRIRA”),
and authorized the U.S. Attorney General (now the DHS Secretary) to “take such actions as may
be necessary to install additional physical barriers and roads . . . in the vicinity of the United States
border to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry into the United States.” P.L. 104-208,
div. C., codified at 8 U.S.C. § 1103 note. In 1996, there were 2.1 apprehensions per border mile
per month in the Big Bend Sector—by far the lowest rates across the entire border. Ex. 1 at 2.
Comparatively, there were over 600 apprehensions per border mile per month in the San Diego
Sector (the sector with the highest per mile apprehensions) and 18.7 apprehensions per border mile
per month in the Yuma Sector (the sector with the second lowest per mile apprehensions that year).
Id. In other words, when Congress passed IIRIRA, the Big Bend Sector was both the sector with
the lowest rates of unlawful entry—about one-ninth of the next-smallest sector in apprehensions
per mile—and a sector with undisputably low rates of unlawful entry. Over the years, this has not
changed.
17.
Further supporting that the Big Bend Sector is not an area of high illegal entry, the
total apprehension figures on which CBP relies strongly appear to overstate the number of
individuals who unlawfully crossed the U.S.-Mexico border within the Sector.
18.
The Big Bend Sector encompasses a large geographic area that includes 77 Texas
counties and all of the State of Oklahoma. According to CBP, the sector covers more than 135,000
square miles.

19.
CBP’s sector-wide apprehension data is not limited to individuals encountered
while unlawfully crossing the international border. Rather, it includes both individuals
apprehended “at entry” and individuals apprehended “at large.” CBP defines an apprehension “at
entry” as involving “an alien who has entered the United States without admission and has not yet
reached his/her destination, regardless of the amount of time since entry.” CBP defines an
apprehension “at large” as involving “an alien who has illegally entered the United States, has
already reached their destination, and is encountered or who was legally admitted and has since
overstayed their permitted time, illegally remaining in the U.S.”
20.
CBP’s apprehension data therefore is not a measure of how many people unlawfully
crossed the U.S.-Mexico border within the Big Bend Sector. Defendants in this case have asserted
that “[b]etween fiscal year 2021 and fiscal year 2025, Border Patrol apprehended over 89,000
illegal aliens attempting to enter the United States between border crossings in the Big Bend
Sector.” Decl. of Paul Enriquez, ECF No. 38-1, ¶ 42. However, that statistic should not be
interpreted as a count of unlawful border crossings occurring within the Big Bend Sector because
the apprehension data reflects encounters occurring through a large enforcement area that extends
beyond the border itself. The figures include individuals encountered throughout the Sector,
regardless of where they crossed the border, as well as individuals who were lawfully admitted but
later encountered within the Sector after overstaying or otherwise lacking lawful status.
21.
To my knowledge, data on “at large” apprehensions broken down by sector is not
publicly available. However, across the U.S.-Mexico border, approximately 3.4% of
apprehensions between Fiscal Years 2024 and 2026 were classified as “at large.” In Fiscal Year
2026 through July 2026, that figure rose to approximately 15.6%. This indicates that a significant
portion of apprehensions involve non-recent border-crossers who may not have crossed the border

174a

8
illegally in the first place. Border Patrol does not offer this data by sector; without more data, there
is no reason to assume that the Big Bend sector varies from the border-wide trend of “at large”
apprehensions.
22.
Additionally, apprehensions at CBP checkpoints are also included in the Sector’s
overall apprehension totals, even though they do not necessarily involve individuals who crossed
the border in the Big Bend Sector. As the U.S. Government Accountability Office (“GAO”)
reported in 2022, Border Patrol maintains “more than 110 checkpoints, located generally 25 to 100
miles from the southwest and northern borders along U.S. highways and secondary roads. All
vehicles traveling through a checkpoint may be subject to a checkpoint inspection.” GAO’s report
included a map, covering 2016-2020, showing four Border Patrol checkpoints in the Big Bend
sector. (https://www.gao.gov/blog/border-patrol-lacks-important-information-about-immigration-
checkpoints-within-united-states)
23.
CBP apprehension data reflects that, between Fiscal Years 2013 and 2025, 12,652
of the 140,654 apprehensions recorded in the Big Bend Sector, or approximately 9%, occurred at
Border Patrol checkpoints. In Fiscal Year 2025, 27.3% of all apprehensions in the Big Bend Sector
occurred at a checkpoint, the highest percentage during the period examined. The lowest
percentage occurred in Fiscal Year 2021, when checkpoint apprehensions accounted for 4.5% of
all apprehensions in the Sector.
24.
Available CBP data further reflects that many individuals apprehended at
checkpoints were present in the U.S. for extended periods of time prior to their apprehension.
Among checkpoint apprehensions in the Big Bend Sector for which the relevant data is publicly
available, 42.7% involved individuals who had been present in the U.S. for more than one month,
and one-third (33%) involved individuals who had been present in the U.S. for more than one year.

DEFENDANTS’ NOTICE REGARDING END OF BIG BEND CONSTRUCTION PAUSE
Defendants respectfully submit this notice to update the Court regarding U.S. Customs and
Border Protection’s (“CBP”) planned activities in the Big Bend 2 and Big Bend 4 project areas
following the expiration of its voluntary pause on ground-disturbing activities. In support of this
notice, Defendants attach the Second Declaration of Paul Enriquez.
I.
Update Regarding the Big Bend 2 Project
Beginning September 30, 2026, CBP will lift the pause on ground disturbing activities for
the Big Bend 2 project. Second Enriquez Decl. ¶ 16. As described in Mr. Enriquez’s first
declaration (ECF No. 38-1), CBP plans to construct approximately 61 miles of barrier system in
Presidio County within this Big Bend Sector. Id. ¶ 17. The system will include a 30-foot bollard
style pedestrian barrier, a road, and, where appropriate for a particular area, cameras, lights,
sensors, and other detection technology. Id.
Most land within the Big Bend 2 project alignment is privately owned. Id. ¶ 18. Before
accessing private property for surveys or other pre-construction work, CBP obtains a right of
access from the landowner. Id. Before constructing border infrastructure, CBP generally acquires
Case 3:26-cv-01099-KC     Document 60     Filed 09/29/26     Page 1 of 5
257a

either a fee interest or an easement in the affected property. Id. As part of that process, CBP
consults with affected landowners and provides them an opportunity to identify concerns. Id. ¶ 19.
Depending on the property, those concerns may include the proposed alignment, continued access
to the Rio Grande, existing irrigation lines, sensitive resources, and other activities conducted on
the property. Id. CBP attempts to accommodate such concerns where possible, including through
the incorporation of access gates into the barrier system. Id.
CBP prefers to acquire the necessary property interest voluntarily. Id. ¶ 20. When a
landowner declines to engage with the government or the parties cannot reach an agreement,
however, CBP may refer the matter to the Department of Justice for a potential condemnation
action.  Id. ¶¶ 20–21. Because a number of landowners in the Big Bend 2 project area have declined
to engage with the government or provide voluntary rights of entry for serving work, CBP
anticipates making a number of such referrals in the coming weeks. Id. ¶ 21.
II.
Update Regarding the Big Bend 4 Project
CBP is actively considering adjustments to the Big Bend 4 project that would reduce its
scope and avoid or minimize potential impacts, based on input received from the National Park
Service and other stakeholders.  Id. ¶ 22.
As previously described, the original project contemplated approximately 17 miles of non-
contiguous vehicle barrier system within and east of Big Bend National Park, construction of a
new patrol road, improvements to existing roads, and the installation of technology within the
National Park.  Id.  Although the Big Bend 4 project area also includes portions of Big Bend Ranch
State Park, CBP does not plan to construct a barrier within the State Park. Id. CBP instead
anticipates constructing a road and associated technology in portions of that area. Id.
CBP expects to make a final decision concerning the revised scope of the Big Bend 4

will promptly update the court and the parties, and CBP will make a public announcement and
